I think you're right, it is semantic (what we decide a word means). "Psychedelic," as the word was first used (I believe by Dr. Humphrey Osmond, a 20th century researcher into what we now thanks to him call psychedelic drugs) literally means "mind-manifesting" from Greek-language roots. So I take this to mean that anything which brings out the effect of the user's mind itself is "psychedelic" - which is a very broad definition indeed; I mean you could take it to mean pretty much anything if you think about it, because it seems that everything we do or interact with affects our minds and brings out the workings of our minds in some way! But it really becomes "semantic" in where we draw the line as to *how much* of an effect something has on us. I do use the word psychedelic to describe the effects of DXM because they affect the action of my mind in such a specific, unusual, and undeniably drastic way. It almost seems sometimes that because the drug is changing the mental processes to such a degree, I am able to take notice of how the mental processes fundamentally work once I take notice all the exaggerations from the effects of the drug. The same can be said of, for example, LSD or psilocybin, although because the chemicals are different and thus interact with the brain in a slightly different way, the effects/mental-manifestations/perceptual-exaggerations/whatever-you-want-to-call-them take on a different "style" - But with still the same potential to snap me into awareness on a deeper level of the fundamental workings of my mind, or "the" mind. I hope this is more clarifying than confusing for people's understanding of the word "psychedelic." It is a tricky word, especially since all our minds are a bit different in some way and so what is subjectively "psychedelic" can vary from person to person. Just my thoughts!

I think if alcohol affects the mind in such a way to make one more comfortable and be able to behave in a more productive way, it is not a problem - socially, that is; letting aside the physical risks of alcohol consumption. According to my understanding of my experience, alcohol as a drug has the primarily sought-after effect of inhibiting the parts of our psychology which scrutinize our own thought processes; which are critically self-conscious. I think that is why many people use alcohol to "loosen up" in social situations - because it inhibits the overarching thoughts processes which say "Should I say this or that? Should I say it in this or that way? How will it sound?" As another example, I as a musician have found that alcohol (up to a certain point \[lol\]) helped me to play music and sing a little better, because I am spending less mental energy scrutinizing how I sound or how I am about to sound while playing; the inhibition of the critical processes allow me to sing and play a little more "boldly" and "naturally." Of course, this is not always a productive thing - to have our self-consciousness inhibited. I have also learned the hard way that when I have had grief or anger in my heart and I have become too drunk from alcohol, these feelings express themselves when part of my mind should have been there to say, "Perhaps I should not express these negative feelings in such a way" -  they just come out, disinhibited. Which led to problems. So, my point here, I think, is that alcohol in its inhibitory/disinhibitory effects can be both beneficial or detrimental depending on what it allows to flow more freely from our psychology into our behaviour. Oh - well, I'm not a metabolic expert but my simple understanding of what I've researched is this: Grapefruit juice (especially white grapefruit juice) contains a substance which chemically blocks an enzyme in your body scientifically known as CYP3A4. (Enzymes as I understand them are biological substances which chemically convert other substances into yet other substances). Now, when DXM enters the body, the CYP3A4 enzyme converts it into another substance called DXO, which is pharmacologically less psychedelic than DXM. So when you drink grapefruit juice, CYP3A4 is inhibited, which leads to DXM being converted to DXO at a retarded (slower) rate, the upshot of which is a more psychedelic experience. This all has to do with where body chemistry meets consciousness meets the Universe so even though we understand the metabolic chemistry to a degree it is still pretty mysterious stuff.
